description: Crowd it and one sweep of ivory clears the road. Otherwise it grazes, wool to the ankles, a herd of one.
lore: Nothing else grazing this country comes anywhere near it for size. Dark brown wool hangs off it nearly to the ankles, the shoulder stands over a grown person, and the tusks come out cream and curve up and out far enough to clear a path on their own. It grazes ground with very little left in it: the molars that come out of one are worn flat past anything grass would account for. What surprises people who expect trouble from something that size is how uninterested it is. Nothing about it is hunting. Nothing about it was ever posted to watch anything. It shifts what is in front of it the way weather shifts things, without attitude, and nearly everything that has ever gone wrong between one of these and a person went wrong because the person stood too close for too long. Crowd it and the head comes round, and one sweep of that ivory ends the conversation.

The spacing is the part to watch. It keeps a gap open on either side of itself. It halts the way an animal halts when the animal ahead of it has halted. It will stand for long stretches in the middle of open ground doing nothing in particular, at the correct interval from nothing in particular. That is herd behaviour, performed accurately, by one animal, and whatever came down out of the sky alongside it is not here to complete the arrangement.

Bringing one down is not like bringing down the small things. The knees go first, and that takes a while. Then it settles into the grass. Then the whole enormous thing goes pale at once, wool and hide and ivory together, while the outline stays exactly where it was — and then the outline goes as well. People who have watched that once do not go out of their way to watch it again, because for a moment it looks like the thing everybody in this country is actually afraid of. It is not that, and the flattened grass is the proof, because there is something lying in it: a piece of ivory small enough to close a hand around, chalk-cream, webbed all over with fine fissures, and warm. The largest thing anybody has met out there comes down to something that fits in a fist, which is either the most even-handed fact in Nangijala or the most unpleasant one, depending on who is holding it. And it could not have been anything else. What this animal knows better than any other is not breaking. The tusks it sheds are snapped clean off at the root by something that never once broke stride, and every fissure in that stone is a break it kept walking after. Set into armour it lends precisely that, which is not strength. It is the habit of continuing while damaged.
